theme: Bidi, hookah, vape and smokeless tobacco (gutka, khaini, zarda, mishri, paan with tobacco)

models.name: Death risk by bidis per day (India, national)
models.estimates: Risk ratio of death from any medical cause at ages 30–69 for Indian men who smoke only bidis, by daily amount, vs non-smokers.
models.output_unit: risk ratio (case-control; adjusted for age, education, alcohol)
models.uncertainty: CIs for these bands are in the Supplementary Appendix (Table 3), not opened; shown as null. P<0.001 for trend.

source.citation: Jha P, Jacob B, Gajalakshmi V, et al. A nationally representative case-control study of smoking and death in India. N Engl J Med 2008;358:1137-47
source.quote: there was a dose–response relationship between smoking and mortality among men who smoked only bidis (risk ratio for one to seven bidis per day, 1.3; risk ratio for eight or more, 2.2)

supporting_sources.citation: Gupta PC, Mehta HC. Cohort study of all-cause mortality among tobacco users in Mumbai, India. Bull World Health Organ 2000;78(7):877-83
supporting_sources.note: Prospective Mumbai cohort, men 35+: bidi smokers age-adjusted RR 1.78; 1–5 bidis/day RR 1.62; 6+/day RR 1.86 (Table 4; no CIs printed). Cigarettes in the same cohort: 1.39 overall, 1.31 and 1.49. Authors: 'bidi smoking as no less hazardous than cigarette smoking'.

models.caveats: Jha 2008 found bidis lower-risk than cigarettes at the same count; the Mumbai cohort found bidis at least as harmful. Both agree even 1–7 bidis a day raises death risk. Show the range honestly ('about 1.3–1.8 times at a few a day'). Most 'any smoking' Indian results in H1 (TB, respiratory, heart) are dominated by bidi smokers, so they apply here too.
models.user_copy: In Indian data, smoking even a few bidis a day was linked to about 1.3–1.6 times the risk of dying early; 8 or more a day, about 1.9–2.2 times.

models.name: How much tobacco is in a bidi vs a cigarette
models.estimates: Tobacco weight per bidi vs per cigarette, and what that does and does not mean for harm.

tobacco_per_bidi.unit: g tobacco per bidi (range printed as 0.15–0.25 g)

models.uncertainty: Descriptive, not a measured toxicant study. The paper states bidis give comparable or higher tar and nicotine despite less tobacco, citing a 1989 Indian review, not its own measurements.

source.citation: Gupta PC, Mehta HC. Cohort study of all-cause mortality among tobacco users in Mumbai, India. Bull World Health Organ 2000;78(7):877-83
source.where: Discussion, p.881 (and Methods description of bidis, p.879)
source.quote: Although a bidi contains a much smaller amount of tobacco (0.2 g) than a cigarette (1 g), it produces a comparable or higher amount of tar and nicotine (4).

supporting_sources.citation: Jha P et al. N Engl J Med 2008;358:1137-47
supporting_sources.note: 'bidis, which are smaller than cigarettes and typically contain only about a quarter as much tobacco, wrapped in the leaf of another plant.'

models.caveats: Do NOT convert bidis to 'cigarette equivalents' by tobacco weight (e.g. 4 bidis = 1 cigarette); the harm data above do not support that. Use bidi-specific risk tables instead. Pack-years must not be computed from bidis.
models.user_copy: A bidi has less tobacco than a cigarette, but it is not a 'lighter' smoke: in Indian studies, even a few bidis a day raised health risks.

models.name: Heart attack risk: bidi, chewing tobacco, both, and per extra cigarette
models.estimates: Odds of a first non-fatal heart attack for different tobacco types vs never users, plus the per-cigarette increase.

per_extra_cigarette_increase.unit: % increase in odds per additional cigarette/day

valid_for.population: 52 countries incl. South Asia; 12,461 cases, 14,637 controls; 1999–2003
valid_for.exposure_range: type-specific rows are current vs never; per-cigarette slope across typical amounts
valid_for.south_asian_validated: partly: includes South Asian sites; bidi row is by definition South Asian

models.uncertainty: 95% CIs printed. Case-control; adjusted for lifestyle confounders. The 5.6% per cigarette is printed without CI in the abstract.

source.citation: Teo KK, Ounpuu S, Hawken S, et al. Tobacco use and risk of myocardial infarction in 52 countries in the INTERHEART study: a case-control study. Lancet 2006;368(9536):647-58
source.quote: Chewing tobacco alone was associated with OR 2.23 (1.41-3.52), and smokers who also chewed tobacco had the highest increase in risk (4.09, 2.98-5.61).

supporting_sources.citation: Jha P et al. N Engl J Med 2008 (India)
supporting_sources.note: Death from heart disease in Indian smokers (mostly bidi): men 1.6 (1.5–1.8), women 1.7 (1.3–2.1), 99% CI.

models.caveats: The per-cigarette slope (+5.6% per extra cigarette) also belongs in H1 as a per-cigarette heart-attack option; if used, compute OR = 1.056^cigs as our own algebra and cap at typical amounts, and note it conflicts in shape with Hackshaw's steep-then-flat curve. Chewing-only row is the best available heart number for smokeless users.
models.user_copy: Chewing tobacco was linked to about 2.2 times the heart attack risk (range 1.4–3.5); smoking and chewing together, about 4 times.

models.name: Mouth cancer from chewing tobacco (South Asia)
models.estimates: Odds / relative risk of oral cavity cancer in users of chewing (smokeless) tobacco of any type vs non-users, and for betel quid without tobacco.

inputs.name: smokeless_portions_per_day
inputs.how_we_get_it: daily log (gutka, khaini, zarda, mishri, paan with tobacco)

valid_for.population: South Asia and the Pacific (mostly India; also Pakistan, Taiwan, Papua New Guinea); studies to June 2013
valid_for.exposure_range: user vs non-user; no pooled dose curve

models.uncertainty: 95% CIs printed. High heterogeneity (I² 75% case-control, 80% cohort). Cohort CI printed as 2.56–11.71 in abstract and 2.57–11.71 in results.

source.citation: Gupta B, Johnson NW. Systematic review and meta-analysis of association of smokeless tobacco and of betel quid without tobacco with incidence of oral cancer in South Asia and the Pacific. PLoS One 2014;9(11):e113385
source.where: Abstract; Results sections for case-control and cohort studies
source.quote: Under the random effects model, the overall estimate for males and females combined together was ORRE = 7.46 (95% CI = 5.86–9.50, P<0.001)

supporting_sources.citation: Guha N, Warnakulasuriya S, Vlaanderen J, Straif K. Betel quid chewing and the risk of oral and oropharyngeal cancers: a meta-analysis with implications for cancer control. Int J Cancer 2014;135(6):1433-43
supporting_sources.note: Indian subcontinent: betel quid WITH tobacco mRR 7.74 (5.38–11.13; 31 studies); WITHOUT tobacco 2.56 (2.00–3.28; 15 studies). IARC authors. Abstract only; exposure-response spline models are in the full text.

models.caveats: The authors say studies powered for dose-response are still needed; the Discussion reports a linear increase with quids/day in individual studies but no pooled slope. Do not show a per-portion number yet. Areca nut itself (supari, pan masala without tobacco) carries risk too, so 'tobacco-free pan masala' is not safe.
models.user_copy: Chewing tobacco is linked to about 5–7 times the risk of mouth cancer (range about 2.6–11). Even paan or supari without tobacco raises it about 2.8 times.

models.name: Paan / betel quid with vs without tobacco (Indian subcontinent)
models.estimates: Meta-relative risk of oral and oropharyngeal cancer for betel quid with tobacco and without tobacco, Indian subcontinent.

valid_for.population: Indian subcontinent studies (31 with tobacco, 15 without)
valid_for.exposure_range: user vs non-user in abstract; spline dose-response by quids/day and years in full text

source.citation: Guha N, Warnakulasuriya S, Vlaanderen J, Straif K. Betel quid chewing and the risk of oral and oropharyngeal cancers: a meta-analysis with implications for cancer control. Int J Cancer 2014;135(6):1433-43
source.quote: The meta-relative risk (mRR) for oral/oropharyngeal cancer in the Indian subcontinent was 2.56 (95%CI, 2.00-3.28; 15 studies) for BQ-T and 7.74 (95%CI, 5.38-11.13; 31 studies) for BQ+T

models.caveats: This is the best candidate for a per-quid dose curve in H2: the paper's exposure-response splines by daily amount and years (full text, not opened) should be pulled next. Overlaps with smokeless-oral-cancer-south-asia; show one or the other, not both stacked.
models.user_copy: Paan with tobacco is linked to about 7–8 times the mouth-cancer risk (range 5–11); without tobacco, about 2.5 times.

models.name: Death risk from smokeless tobacco by type and times per day (Mumbai)
models.estimates: Age-adjusted relative risk of death from any cause for smokeless tobacco users vs non-users, by product and daily frequency.
models.output_unit: age-adjusted relative risk (ratio of age-adjusted death rates)

valid_for.population: Mumbai (main city), baseline 1991–1994, follow-up to 1999; 52,568 people; 4,358 deaths

models.uncertainty: No CIs printed; relative risks are ratios of age-adjusted rates only (not adjusted for alcohol, education etc.). Some cells small (e.g. women mishri 6+ = 2,786 person-years).

source.citation: Gupta PC, Mehta HC. Cohort study of all-cause mortality among tobacco users in Mumbai, India. Bull World Health Organ 2000;78(7):877-83
source.quote: Smokeless tobacco use was very high among men and women, the age-adjusted relative risk for men (1096 deaths) being 1.22 and for women (1575 deaths) 1.35.

supporting_sources.citation: Gupta PC, Pednekar MS, Parkin DM, Sankaranarayanan R. Tobacco associated mortality in Mumbai (Bombay) India. Results of the Bombay Cohort Study. Int J Epidemiol 2005;34:1395-1402
supporting_sources.note: Larger follow-up (99,570 people, 7,531 deaths) of the same cohort; its relative risks were not visible in the abstract fragment I read. Use this as the preferred update once opened.

models.caveats: Modest, age-adjusted-only estimates; authors call the smokeless findings 'slightly more difficult to interpret'. Mishri (roasted tobacco powder rubbed on gums, often used as tooth powder) is common in Maharashtra; gutka/khaini were not separately analysed. Pair with cancer and heart models rather than showing alone.
models.user_copy: In a Mumbai study, people who used chewing or gum-rubbing tobacco several times a day had about 1.2–1.5 times the risk of dying early.

models.name: One hookah session vs one cigarette: smoke, nicotine, tar, CO
models.estimates: Inhaled smoke volume, nicotine, tar and carbon monoxide per hookah session and per cigarette (pooled lab and café measurements).
models.formula: nicotine_mg = hookah_sessions * 4.1; tar_mg = hookah_sessions * 619; co_mg = hookah_sessions * 192; smoke_litres = hookah_sessions * 74.1

valid_for.population: 17 laboratory / café studies (mostly Lebanon, USA, Germany); published before April 2013
valid_for.exposure_range: a full session (typically ~45 minutes, 10–20 g moist tobacco per bowl)

models.uncertainty: 95% CIs printed; very high heterogeneity (all p<0.001). Most tar/nicotine values from machine protocols; authors found human and machine studies similar.

source.citation: Primack BA, Carroll MV, Weiss PM, et al. Systematic review and meta-analysis of inhaled toxicants from waterpipe and cigarette smoking. Public Health Rep 2016;131(1):76-85

models.caveats: Ratios from the same table: about 25x tar, ~11x CO, ~2.3x nicotine and ~120x smoke per session vs one cigarette (our division of the printed means). The authors warn this is exposure, not disease risk, and that per-session vs per-cigarette is an imperfect comparison. Do NOT turn sessions into 'cigarette-equivalents' for disease risk. Indian 'herbal' / nicotine-free hookah still produces CO and tar from charcoal (charcoal is the main CO source per the authors).
models.user_copy: One hookah session is about as much nicotine as 2 cigarettes, but roughly 25 times the tar and 10 times the carbon monoxide of one cigarette.

models.name: Hookah and disease (pooled associations)
models.estimates: Odds ratios for diseases significantly associated with waterpipe smoking vs non-use.

inputs.name: uses_hookah
inputs.how_we_get_it: any hookah logged in last 30 days

valid_for.population: 50 studies (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional), searched to May 2015; mostly Middle East and South/East Asia
valid_for.south_asian_validated: partly: some included studies from South Asia; not separated in abstract

models.uncertainty: 95% CIs printed; many are wide. Mix of designs, including cross-sectional.

source.citation: Waziry R, Jawad M, Ballout RA, Al Akel M, Akl EA. The effects of waterpipe tobacco smoking on health outcomes: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis. Int J Epidemiol 2017;46(1):32-43
source.quote: oral cancer OR=4.17, 95% CI=2.53, 6.89; lung cancer OR=2.12, 95% CI=1.32, 3.42

supporting_sources.citation: Teo KK et al. INTERHEART, Lancet 2006
supporting_sources.note: Conclusion: all forms of tobacco, including different types of smoking, harm the heart (sheesha specifically mentioned in secondary coverage, not in the abstract read).

models.caveats: Not significant (so do not show as harm numbers): oesophageal cancer, gastric cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, mortality. Evidence is 'user vs non-user' only, so no per-session dose.
models.user_copy: Regular hookah use is linked to about 2 times the lung cancer risk (range 1.3–3.4) and about 4 times the mouth cancer risk (range 2.5–6.9).

models.name: E-cigarettes: what is and isn't known
models.estimates: Evidence levels for health effects of e-cigarettes, for honest 'not enough evidence' messaging.

table.finding: Heart rate increases shortly after nicotine intake from e-cigarettes
Diastolic blood pressure increases after nicotine intake
Acute endothelial (blood-vessel lining) dysfunction from aerosol
Complete switching from cigarettes reduces exposure to many toxicants and carcinogens
Youth who vape are more likely to start smoking cigarettes

models.uncertainty: Qualitative evidence grades; no numeric risk available for long-term disease.

source.citation: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. Public Health Consequences of E-Cigarettes. Washington, DC: National Academies Press; 2018
source.where: Summary Annex, 'Report Conclusions by Level of Evidence' (Conclusions 9-1, 9-2, 9-3, 8-1, 7-1, 18-1)
source.quote: Conclusion 9-2. There is substantial evidence that heart rate increases shortly after nicotine intake from e-cigarettes.

supporting_sources.citation: The Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes (Production, Manufacture, Import, Export, Transport, Sale, Distribution, Storage and Advertisement) Act, 2019 (No. 42 of 2019), Government of India
supporting_sources.note: Legal context: production, import, sale, distribution, storage and advertisement of e-cigarettes (including heat-not-burn and e-hookahs, per PRS summary) are prohibited in India since 18 September 2019.

models.caveats: 'Not enough evidence' is the honest answer for long-term vaping harm; the report is from 2018 and newer evidence was not searched in this pass. In India vaping products are illegal to sell or store (not a health model, but relevant: the app should log vaping without judgement and avoid anything that looks like promotion or sourcing advice). Do not compute 'minutes of life' or disease risk for vaping.
models.user_copy: Vaping raises your heart rate right after use and is addictive. Long-term effects on heart disease and cancer are not known yet.

models.name: How Indians use tobacco (GATS-2, 2016–17)
models.estimates: National prevalence of smoking, bidi, cigarette and smokeless tobacco use among adults 15+ (for defaults and context, not personal risk).

valid_for.population: India, nationally representative household survey, 74,037 people, Aug 2016–Feb 2017

models.uncertainty: Survey estimates; CIs are in the full GATS-2 report (not opened).

source.citation: Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, Government of India. Global Adult Tobacco Survey (GATS-2) India 2016-17, Fact Sheet

supporting_sources.citation: PRS Legislative Research. Legislative Brief: Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes Ordinance, 2019
supporting_sources.note: Source of the 0.02% e-cigarette-user figure (citing GATS 2016-17).

models.caveats: Context only (e.g. to order product options in the logger: smokeless and bidi before cigarettes). Not a personal risk. GATS-2 is from 2016–17; a newer GATS was not searched.
models.user_copy: About 1 in 5 Indian adults uses chewing tobacco and about 1 in 10 smokes. You're not alone, and many are trying to quit.

not_found.reason: Only a descriptive statement (bidi 0.2 g tobacco, 'comparable or higher' tar and nicotine) citing a 1989 Indian review; no laboratory meta-analysis opened this pass.

not_found.reason: Gupta & Johnson 2014 say pooled dose-response data are lacking; Guha 2014 has spline curves for betel quid in the full text (not opened).

not_found.wanted: IARC Monographs vol. 89 / 100E (smokeless tobacco) classification text
not_found.reason: Not opened in this pass; both meta-analyses above rely on IARC material.

not_found.wanted: Smokeless tobacco and oesophagus / pancreas cancer, stroke
not_found.reason: Not searched in this pass; Mumbai cohort site-specific incidence paper (Pednekar 2011, Cancer Causes Control, PMC3756904) is the next source to open.

not_found.wanted: Bombay Cohort 2005 (IJE) updated relative risks by tobacco type
not_found.reason: Only the abstract header was visible; numbers not seen.

not_found.wanted: Hookah dose-response (per session / week) for disease
not_found.reason: Pooled evidence is user vs non-user only.
NASEM 2018: no available evidence; newer (2019–2026) cohort evidence not searched in this pass.

not_found.wanted: 'Equivalent to N cigarettes' claims for bidi / hookah
not_found.reason: Deliberately not modelled: tobacco-weight or single-toxicant equivalences are not validated against disease outcomes.

recommend: Show first: (1) smokeless-oral-cancer-south-asia (or paan-with-tobacco-oral-cancer-india) — India-specific, full text, huge relative risk, and chewing is India's most common tobacco habit per GATS-2. (2) tobacco-type-heart-attack-interheart — gives chewers and bidi smokers a heart number, and the 'smoke + chew = ~4x' row is a strong nudge for dual users. (3) bidi-dose-allcause-india with the Mumbai cohort alongside — directly answers 'bidi is lighter, right?'. (4) hookah-toxicants-per-session — clear, measured per-session numbers for young urban users. (5) vape-evidence-status — honest 'not known yet' copy plus Indian legal context. Also flag for H1: INTERHEART's +5.6% heart-attack odds per extra cigarette is a per-cigarette slope you may want next to Hackshaw.
